items.prompt: HR specialists now need to read audit logs. With the permission-to-roles matrix, what is the minimal correct change?
items.answer: Add HR_SPECIALIST to VIEW_AUDIT_LOGS in PermissionMatrix; no route changes are needed
distractors: Add an if (user.role === 'HR_SPECIALIST') branch inside the audit-log controller, next to the existing admin check
Change every audit route from requirePermission to requireRole and list HR_SPECIALIST in each route's role array
Give HR specialists the SYSTEM_ADMIN role, since the matrix cannot be extended
items.explanation: The matrix maps permission to allowed roles, so adding a role to a permission is a one-line matrix edit; hard-coding role checks in controllers is the pitfall the guide warns about.

items.prompt: When does requirePermission('CREATE_ONBOARDING_CASE') look up the allowed roles in PermissionMatrix?
items.answer: Once, when the route is registered: the lookup runs outside the handler that requireRole returns
distractors: On every request, inside the returned middleware, so runtime edits to the matrix apply immediately
Lazily on the first request, then cached per user
Never: the permission string is compared directly against the user's role
items.explanation: requirePermission reads PermissionMatrix[permission] in its own body and passes the array to requireRole, which closes over it; the guide stresses this happens at route-registration time.

items.prompt: According to PermissionMatrix, which permission does the MANAGER role hold?
distractors: VIEW_REPORTS and APPROVE_MANAGER_STEP
VIEW_ALL_CASES, so managers can list every department's cases
COMPLETE_IT_TASK, shared with IT_ADMIN
items.explanation: MANAGER appears in exactly one matrix entry, APPROVE_MANAGER_STEP (alongside SYSTEM_ADMIN); IT_ADMIN alone (with SYSTEM_ADMIN) holds COMPLETE_IT_TASK.

items.prompt: The guide's department-scoped findUnique snippet is labeled 'Illustrative, not from the repo'. Reading the real router, what protects GET /cases/:id?
items.answer: Only authMiddleware: any authenticated user can request any case id, with no permission or department check on that route
distractors: requirePermission('VIEW_ALL_CASES'), which limits it to admins and HR
A departmentId filter appended by authMiddleware to every Prisma query
validate(createOnboardingCaseSchema), which rejects ids from other departments
items.explanation: router.use(authMiddleware) applies to every route, but GET '/:id' adds no requirePermission; the scoping pattern the guide recommends is not applied here, which is exactly the IDOR shape it describes.

items.prompt: While starting an onboarding case, the final tx.auditEvent.create fails. What state is the database left in?
items.answer: Unchanged: the generated tasks, the status update and the activity row all roll back
distractors: The tasks and the IN_PROGRESS status update persist, and only the compliance audit event is missing
The case is IN_PROGRESS with zero tasks, because task rows are written after the audit event
Everything persists and the audit write is retried later by the notification queue
items.explanation: All writes in startOnboardingCase go through the interactive transaction client tx, so a failed audit write aborts the whole unit: either the action and its audit trail both exist, or neither does.

items.prompt: Why does the controller send the onboarding-started notification only after startOnboardingCase resolves, wrapped in its own try/catch?
items.answer: So no slow external call runs inside the transaction, and a notification failure cannot undo a committed start
distractors: Because Prisma forbids dynamic import() calls inside $transaction callbacks and would throw at runtime
So the welcome email can still be rolled back if the transaction later fails to commit
Because the notification needs the audit event's id, which only exists after a second transaction commits
items.explanation: The guide's rule is never to run external calls inside a transaction (latency ties up connections). The controller enqueues after commit and only logs a warning if enqueuing fails.

items.prompt: Redis is down. An email notification is recorded as PENDING and handed to the in-memory fallback, then the Node process restarts 200 ms later. What happens to that email?
items.answer: It is never delivered automatically: the setTimeout job lived only in memory, so the row stays PENDING
distractors: BullMQ replays it from Redis once Redis comes back, because the job was written to the queue before the fallback
It is delivered at boot, because server startup re-queues every PENDING email row it finds
It was already sent synchronously before the timeout was scheduled
items.explanation: The fallback schedules deliverEmailMock with setTimeout(…, 500). The critique notes pending notifications are lost on crash or restart: zero durability or retry persistence.

items.prompt: A case has 6 tasks: 2 COMPLETED, 1 SKIPPED, 2 TODO and 1 PENDING_APPROVAL. What progressPercent does recalculateOnboardingProgress store?
items.explanation: COMPLETED and SKIPPED both count as done: 3 of 6, Math.round(0.5 * 100) = 50. PENDING_APPROVAL does not count.

items.prompt: A COMPLETED case has a task moved back to TODO, and progress is recalculated to 80%. What happens to the case, given that the state machine lists COMPLETED with no allowed transitions?
items.answer: The progress service sets status to IN_PROGRESS directly and keeps the original completedAt, bypassing validateCaseTransition
distractors: validateCaseTransition throws INVALID_STATE_TRANSITION and the task update fails
The case stays COMPLETED with 80% progress, because COMPLETED is terminal
The case becomes IN_PROGRESS and completedAt is reset to null
items.explanation: recalculateOnboardingProgress writes data.status = 'IN_PROGRESS' when the current status is COMPLETED and progress is below 100, and never nulls completedAt; it does not consult the state machine.

items.prompt: The guide says every task status update recalculates progress 'inside the same transaction block'. What does the direct status path of the task service actually do?
items.answer: Updates the task, logs activity, then recalculates progress as separate non-transactional calls, so progress can go stale
distractors: It wraps the task update and the recalculation in prisma.$transaction, exactly as the guide describes, so the column never drifts
It never recalculates progress on this path; only approval decisions call recalculateOnboardingProgress
It recalculates progress before updating the task, so the stored value is always one step behind
items.explanation: On the direct path, prisma.onboardingTask.update, the activity create and recalculateOnboardingProgress(task.onboardingCaseId) are called on the base client with no tx, so the materialized column can drift if a later call fails.

items.prompt: A user logs out, but an attacker has already copied their access token. How long can the attacker keep calling the API?
items.answer: Until the access token expires (15 minutes by default): there is no revocation list
distractors: Not at all: logout deletes the token server-side, so the next call fails signature verification
For 7 days, because access tokens are issued with the same lifetime as the refresh token
Until the user's next login, which rotates JWT_ACCESS_SECRET
items.explanation: verifyAccessToken is jwt.verify with the access secret; with no blacklist, a cryptographically valid token works until JWT_ACCESS_EXPIRES_IN (default '15m') elapses.

items.prompt: Several HR managers start onboarding workflows at the same moment on the SQLite deployment. What failure does the critique predict?
items.answer: Writers queue behind SQLite's single write lock, so some requests stall and fail with SQLITE_BUSY
distractors: Dirty reads, where one manager sees another manager's uncommitted tasks before the start transaction commits
Duplicate primary keys, because SQLite cannot generate ids for concurrent inserts safely
Silent lost updates, because SQLite has no transactions
items.explanation: SQLite supports one concurrent writer; the multi-write start transaction holds the lock, and with no retry logic (critique item 3) the error escapes to the client.

items.front: GET /cases/:id has only authMiddleware and fetches the case by raw id. Risk and fix?
items.back: IDOR: any authenticated user can read any department's case by changing the id. Fix: scope the query with the departmentId resolved from the verified session (or require VIEW_ALL_CASES), and add a cross-department security test.

items.front: Trade-off of storing progressPercent instead of computing it on read?
items.back: Reads and sorting are fast (a plain integer column), but every write path that changes tasks must recalculate it, ideally in the same transaction; any path that skips or fails the hook leaves the column stale.

items.front: When Redis is offline, notifications fall back to setTimeout in the Node process. Risk and fix?
items.back: Pending jobs die with the process (crash, OOM, autoscale restart): no durability, no retry. In production, refuse to boot without the queue, or sweep PENDING email rows on startup.

items.front: Rule for side effects such as emails around a database transaction?
items.back: Keep them out of the transaction: commit first, then enqueue. External latency inside a transaction holds connections and locks, and a side effect cannot be rolled back with the data.
